tagline: Sandstone, mesas and longleaf pines mark seventeen miles through Kisatchie.
intro: Longleaf Trail Byway follows Forest Road 59 for 17 miles through Kisatchie National Forest, linking Highway 117 on the west with Highway 119 on the east. Elevations range from 80 to 400 feet above sea level. Louisiana’s tourism office describes this as rugged terrain by the state’s standards, with outlooks onto mesas, buttes, sandstone outcrops and longleaf pines. Its byway itinerary allows up to half a day for a self-guided tour. The forest includes pine-covered hills and hardwood bottoms, with the wilderness beside this drive forming one of its large roadless areas.

Federal land purchases began in 1911, after timber companies had clear-cut much of the area. Caroline Dormon, a former teacher who joined Louisiana’s forestry department, sought protection for remaining old-growth forest. She wrote officials and attended meetings; a tract was selected for protection in 1929. Kisatchie National Forest was designated in 1930.

From Highway 117, the drive begins at the ranger-station end and follows the southern side of Kisatchie Hills Wilderness. Longleaf Vista comes four miles before Highway 119, with the wilderness surrounding the overlook on three sides. Here a 1.5-mile interpretive loop passes through meadows and bottomland hardwoods to high mesas and creeks. The road continues east to Highway 119.
notice: Look for sandstone outcrops and longleaf pines from the byway’s outlooks.

moments.title: Kisatchie Bayou
moments.text: White sand and rocky rapids mark Kisatchie Bayou Recreation Area. The bayou runs through a large portion of the national forest and is a tributary of Old River at Isle Brevelle. The recreation area provides camping and day use beside that water. A separate route through the forest, the 10.5-mile Caroline Dormon Hiking and Horse Trail, leads to Kisatchie Bayou Camp. Evergreen Southern magnolias line the bayou’s banks.

moments.title: Kisatchie Hills Wilderness
moments.text: The road borders Kisatchie Hills Wilderness, but travel inside the wilderness is on foot or horseback. Its 8,701 acres preserve terrain unusually rugged for Louisiana. The seven-mile Backbone Trail crosses the area, with two shorter spur trails branching from it. Bayou Cypre drains the wilderness through a network of tributary streams and crosses its eastern boundary. Walking the complete Backbone Trail requires wading that sand-bottomed stream. The Forest Service manages the wilderness within Kisatchie National Forest; the byway borders its southern and southwestern sides, separating the drive from the roadless interior.

moments.title: Longleaf Vista
moments.text: Longleaf Vista looks into Kisatchie Hills Wilderness, which surrounds the overlook on three sides. The recreation area sits four miles west of Highway 119, near the eastern end of the drive. Its sandstone bluffs belong to a landscape of mesas, buttes and longleaf pines. The 1.5-mile interpretive loop follows that changing terrain through meadows and bottomland hardwoods to high mesas and creeks. The surrounding wilderness is known locally as “Little Grand Canyon.” Visitors have found small fossils and petrified wood here, details on a different scale from the overlook’s mesas.
